fields.v: Zhou, X., Chen, V., Wang, Z. Z., Neubig, G., Sap, M., Wang, X. (2026). ToM-SWE: User Mental Modeling for Software Engineering Agents. arXiv:2510.21903v2 [cs.SE], 29 Jan 2026
Preprint (arXiv; 'Preprint. February 2, 2026')
Language Technology Institute, Carnegie Mellon University; All Hands AI (company behind OpenHands, the platform the approach is built on)

Proposes an approach (ToM-SWE: dual-agent SWE agent + theory-of-mind agent with persistent user memory) and evaluates/compares it against CodeAct and RAG baselines (secondary: proposes an evaluation method, the Stateful SWE benchmark with profile-conditioned user simulators)

ToM-SWE, implemented as ToMCodeAct agent on OpenHands (version Not stated). Baselines: OpenHands CodeAct agent; RAGCodeAct (CodeAct prompted to retrieve past sessions via BM25). Human study used a ToM-enhanced OpenHands CLI

No specification artefacts. Three-tier external user memory: (1) raw session storage; (2) session-based user model (JSON: session intent, interaction patterns, coding preferences); (3) overall user model (JSON: profile, interaction style, coding preferences, session summaries). ToM suggestions with confidence score

In-session: SWE agent decides to call consult_tom -> ToM agent reads/searches memory (max 3 actions) -> give_suggestions -> SWE agent adapts action. After-session: update_memory -> analyze_session (tier 2) -> initialize/update overall user model (tier 3)
None prescribed in the flow. In the human study developers marked each ToM suggestion Accept / Almost right (modify) / Reject. Benchmarks: simulated user answers clarification questions
Full workflow (both in-session and after-session ToM) in benchmarks and in the 3-week field study
Not classifiable (no specification; user mental model memory, not a spec)
Existing code base (SWE-bench Verified issues turned into vague instructions; field study: developers' own daily tasks)
Ambiguous SWE-bench and Stateful SWE-bench: 500 instances each, max 100 interaction turns; cost study 100 sampled instances; field study 209 sessions, 174 ToM suggestions. Repository size Not stated
Python open-source repositories (SWE-bench); field study: developers' own work, not described (privacy)
Benchmarks: GPT-5 user simulators conditioned on 15 developer profiles derived from 453 real OpenHands sessions. Field study: 17 professional developers, 3 weeks, CLI
Average session cost (USD) of the ToM agent per base model and ToM overhead as % of average SWE session cost ($1.08) (100 instances only). No token or time metrics
Task resolved rate (% of instances passing SWE-bench unit tests)
None
None measured directly; field study measured acceptance of ToM suggestions (accept / partial / reject)

User simulator satisfaction score (1-5; overall, communication, problem solving, efficiency, preference alignment); F+H rate (failed but high satisfaction); correlation resolution vs satisfaction; suggestion acceptance rate by query category

Automatic: unit tests; LLM (GPT-5) profile-conditioned simulator ratings (validated on 30 samples vs human, r = 0.86); cost from API usage. Field study: in-CLI developer annotations of each suggestion. Manual analysis of 44 F+H cases and 50 sampled suggestions

Criterion: resolved rate on SWE-bench tests; satisfaction; acceptance. All benchmark runs on OpenHands; ToM agent model Claude Sonnet 4 in all benchmark runs.

Tasks: 500 SWE-bench Verified instances in Ambiguous SWE-bench and Stateful SWE-bench (15 profiles). Configurations: CodeAct vs RAGCodeAct vs ToMCodeAct x 3 SWE models (Claude Sonnet 4, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Qwen3-480B). Baseline: CodeAct. Held constant: OpenHands platform, same simulated users, same prompt (Listing 8), ToM model Claude Sonnet 4, BM25 retrieval top-3, temperatures 0.1 ToM / 0.7 SWE. Acceptance tests: SWE-bench unit tests. Repetitions: Not stated (single run apparently). Human intervention: none (simulated users). Field study observational, no control group

ToMCodeAct best on resolved rate and satisfaction for all models: Ambiguous +11.5 pp (63.4 vs 51.9, Claude 4); Stateful +41.6 pp (59.7 vs 18.1, Claude 4); satisfaction 3.62 vs 2.57 (+41%). RAG below ToM for all models, and below CodeAct with Claude 3.7 (14.4 vs 18.7). Significance of differences not tested (only ± values in Table 1); resolution-satisfaction correlation r = 0.74, p < 0.001

Distinguished configurations clearly on Stateful benchmark; repeatability not assessed (no repetitions). Limitations stated: LLM user simulator may introduce systematic biases (mitigated by calibration and 30-sample manual check); field study observational, no causal productivity claims

Simulator bias (over-knowledgeability, excessive compliance); privacy and consent of user modeling; profiles mainly English-speaking developers, limited diversity; generalisation beyond SE open; ToM struggles with very vague queries and low-confidence cases; how to leverage user effort is open
